Postgres query excludes only pg_catalog/information_schema namespaces (235), covering extension functions; MySQL query restricts to ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION' (244). docs/external/row-level-security.md:164 contains the quoted text. PostgreSQL docs (xfunc-sql, 'SQL Functions on Composite Types') say a function taking a composite/table row type can be called as attribute notation `table.function` (e.g. `SELECT o.order_total FROM orders o` resolves to order_total(o)) when no column of that name exists. PostgreSQL's GRANT/default privileges docs say EXECUTE on functions is granted to PUBLIC by default, so revoking it from PUBLIC is the right instruction. Both are from my knowledge of the PostgreSQL docs; I did not fetch them in this run. The claim is an authored doc statement, and it is accurate.

I found no dedicated test for the MySQL PARTITION clause (grep of tests found none), and I did not run the code. The conclusion rests on reading the parser and rls.py. Caveat: the sqlglot checked is the repo's .venv copy, not necessarily the version pinned for CI.

Docstring at relations.py:117-120 matches the code path (_called_names 84-107 feeding _refuse_database_routines 222-252, run even with no relations at 125-132). Open risk not settled by reading: sqlglot Postgres tokenizer only supports U&' string escapes (sqlglot/dialects/postgres.py:90), so a Unicode-escaped quoted identifier call such as U&"\0066n"(1) would likely tokenize to VAR U, &, IDENTIFIER with raw text \0066n, which would not match the routine fn that PostgreSQL decodes to; likewise MySQL routine names use an accent-insensitive collation while the match is LOWER(...) IN (...) on exact text. I did not run parse_one/tokenize or a live database to confirm these, and I did not confirm that the read-only guard lets such statements through, so neither FAIL nor PASS is established.

relations.py:91-92 docstring says PostgreSQL folds only ASCII in unquoted names; relations.py:104-106 adds text as written, text.lower() and an ASCII-only-lowered form (ch.lower() if ch.isascii() else ch) to the names set, so the code matches the claim. rls.py:196-200 treats non-ASCII unquoted folding as encoding/locale dependent. PostgreSQL's downcase_identifier folds only ASCII in multibyte encodings but may tolower high-bit chars in single-byte encodings; the docstring simplifies that, but the Python lower() form in the set covers that case, so matching is not weakened (wording imprecision only, suggestion level).

relations.py:165-172 SELECT returns c.relkind, n.nspname, c.relname, EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM pg_catalog.pg_inherits i WHERE i.inhrelid = c.oid): four columns in that order. row[0] is kind, row[1:3] is (nspname, relname), row[3] is the child flag (line 178), so indexing matches. pg_inherits.inhrelid is the OID of the child table (inhparent is the parent), so the EXISTS is true for partitions and inheritance children. EXISTS yields PostgreSQL boolean, which psycopg2's default BOOLEAN typecaster returns as Python bool. The code also checks isinstance(is_child, bool) at lines 179-184 and fails closed otherwise. This rests on the documented catalog and psycopg2 behavior, not on a run against a live database.

relations.py:240-247 builds one '%s' per name, joined by ', ', and executes 'SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.ROUTINES WHERE ROUTINE_TYPE = 'FUNCTION' AND LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN (...) LIMIT 1' with tuple(names), which is pymysql's format paramstyle. The caller (relations.py:124-132) only calls it when `called` is non-empty, so IN () cannot occur. This is from the MySQL docs as I recall them, not re-fetched here. The docstring at 222-230 states the name-only matching.
